title: Find Duplicate Subtrees
description:
# Find Duplicate Subtrees

Given the `root` of a binary tree, return the roots of all **duplicate subtree kinds**.

Two subtrees are duplicates when they have exactly the same structure and the same node values at every corresponding position. Missing children are part of the structure, so `[2,3]` and `[2,null,3]` are different subtrees.

For each duplicate kind, return the root of any one occurrence. The answer may be returned in any order.

Example trees use a level-order display: list the root, then each existing node's left and right children in node order. `null` means an absent child; trailing nulls may be omitted. A tree node stores `val`, `left`, and `right`; tree parameters or return values in code are `TreeNode` objects.

## Example 1:

**Input:** root = [1,2,3,4,null,2,4,null,null,4]
**Output:** [[2,4],[4]]
**Explanation:** The subtree rooted at value `2` with left child `4` appears twice, and the leaf subtree `4` appears three times.

## Example 2:

**Input:** root = [2,1,1]
**Output:** [[1]]

## Example 3:

**Input:** root = [2,2,2,3,null,3,null]
**Output:** [[2,3],[3]]

## Constraints:

* The number of nodes in the tree is in the range `[1, 5000]`.
* `-200 <= Node.val <= 200`.

solutions.name: Postorder String Serialization
solutions.description:
## Approach

Serialize every subtree with postorder DFS. A signature includes the node value, the left subtree signature, and the right subtree signature. Count each signature in a hash map and add a root to the answer exactly when its signature is seen for the second time.

## Key Insight

Null markers are mandatory. Without them, different shapes can collapse to the same string. Postorder works well because a node can form its own complete signature only after both child signatures are known.

## Complexity Analysis

There are `n` signatures, and each signature can be proportional to the size of its subtree in the worst case.

- Time Complexity: O(n^2)
- Space Complexity: O(n^2)

solutions.name: Canonical Integer IDs
solutions.description:
## Approach

Assign an integer ID to every unique `(node value, left ID, right ID)` triple. Count IDs instead of long subtree strings, and add a root when its ID appears for the second time.

## Key Insight

The triple ID is a canonical name for the whole subtree. Once equal child subtrees already have equal IDs, equal triples are exactly equal subtrees. This removes repeated long-string construction and hashing.

## Complexity Analysis

Each node creates and looks up one constant-size key.

- Time Complexity: O(n)
- Space Complexity: O(n)

solutions.name: Structural Equality Buckets
solutions.description:
## Approach

Use direct tree comparison as a baseline. Group previously seen subtree roots by their root value. For a new root, compare it only with candidates from the same value bucket, and report the duplicate kind only the first time a second occurrence is found.

## Key Insight

This is slower, but it is useful pedagogically because it checks the definition without serialization. The root-value buckets avoid many impossible comparisons while still preserving correctness.

## Complexity Analysis

Many equal-valued roots can force repeated structural comparisons in the worst case.

- Time Complexity: O(n^2)
- Space Complexity: O(n)
